metadata.note: The Denver & Rio Grande's narrow-gauge Santa Fe Branch, universally nicknamed the 'Chili Line' for the chile-pepper crop local farmers shipped on it, ran 125.6 miles from Antonito, CO (junction with the D&RG's San Juan Extension toward Chama/Durango) south to Santa Fe, NM, via Tres Piedras, Embudo, and Espanola. Built by Palmer's D&RG south from Antonito, reaching Espanola December 30, 1880 (a few sources instead say through service from that end only began 1881); the remaining ~34 miles Espanola-Santa Fe were built by an independent company, the Texas, Santa Fe & Northern Railroad, and finished January 8, 1887 (an excursion train ran January 9, 1887). That southern piece passed through the Santa Fe Southern Railway (1889) and the Rio Grande & Santa Fe Railroad (a D&RG-controlled unit by 1895) before formally merging into its parent August 1, 1908; for map purposes it is treated as D&RG-operated for the whole of its pre-1921 life, since D&RG controlled it for all but its first eight years. The Denver and Rio Grande Western Railroad took formal control of the whole D&RG system August 1, 1921 in a bankruptcy reorganization -- a genuine ownership change, not just a rebranding -- so each geographic piece of this line is split into a pre-1921 D&RG feature and a 1921-1941 D&RGW feature, all four sharing this file's traced geometry in pairs. Passenger/mixed service ran the whole route (trains #425/#426 in the final years) until the Rio Grande, having received ICC abandonment permission in January 1941, made its last run September 1, 1941 -- one of narrow-gauge railroading's most famous abandonments, described by a Time magazine correspondent watching 'a little group of mourners' see the final train off from the Santa Fe depot while the city's fiesta crowds slept elsewhere. Track was pulled up within days; the line was fully dismantled by 1942 and a good deal of its rail and rolling stock went to Alaska for wartime construction. Two branches documented off this route -- No Agua to Stewart Junction, and a ~16-mile branch from Taos Junction to La Madera (built 1914, serving a lumber mill that closed 1927) -- are not traced on this map.
sources: https://time.com/archive/6765400/new-mexico-end-of-the-chili-line/ (Time magazine's 1941 contemporary account of the last run)

OpenStreetMap (via Overpass API): railway=abandoned/disused/razed ways tagged 'Chili Line' / 'Chilli Line' / 'Chili Line (D&RG)' with old_railway_operator=Denver & Rio Grande, running Antonito CO - Tres Piedras - Embudo - Espanola - Santa Fe NM
geometry_sources: OpenStreetMap (via Overpass API, overpass-api.de), queried for railway=rail/narrow_gauge/abandoned/disused/razed ways in a bounding box covering Antonito CO south to Santa Fe NM. OSM tags a large fraction of this closed-1941 grade directly as 'Chili Line', 'Chilli Line', or 'Chili Line (D&RG)', many carrying old_railway_operator=Denver & Rio Grande -- far better preserved in OSM than expected for a line abandoned this long ago. Fragments were stitched into a routing graph (nodes snapped to 5 decimal places, Dijkstra shortest path over haversine edge weights) from Antonito to Santa Fe; the graph was manually pruned first to drop the Cumbres & Toltec corridor west of Antonito (a different D&RG line, to Chama) and an unnamed disconnected D&RG-tagged fragment far to the west near 36.21N/106.3W that does not lie on this route. Where the real-tagged fragments do not connect, the route uses a straight-line bridge between the nearest fragment endpoints -- see each feature's geometry_quality for the size and location of every such bridge. Total traced length (both features combined) is 122.65 miles against the documented 125.6 miles (97.6%); the shortfall is ordinary route-following/curve-simplification, not a missing stretch. A backtrack/self-intersection check (cumulative along-path distance vs. direct distance for every point pair at least 500m apart along the route, flagging any pair under 250m apart) found zero flags across the full 1875-point path -- no out-and-back retracing.
metadata.not_yet_sourced: Whether the Antonito-Espanola opening is better dated to December 1880 (american-rails.com) or 1881 (chililinedepot.com) is unresolved -- sources conflict and neither cites a primary document here. Real timetable frequency is only documented for the final years (mixed trains #425/#426); headway for the 1880s-1930s is an unsourced estimate. The Stewart Junction and La Madera branches are not traced. The exact route through the town of Espanola itself (where OSM has no rail tagging at all) is a straight-line bridge rather than a traced street- or right-of-way-level alignment.

segments.note: The D&RG's narrow-gauge Santa Fe Branch reached Espanola from Antonito December 30, 1880, completing this ~92-mile northern two-thirds of the eventual Chili Line through Tres Piedras and Embudo (some sources instead date through operation from this end to 1881). Mixed passenger/freight service; frequency is an unsourced estimate.

properties.geometry_quality: Real-traced from OpenStreetMap for ~17.1 of this feature's ~30.9 miles (55.4%) -- this southern, canyon-country half of the line is far more poorly preserved in OSM's abandoned-rail tagging than the Antonito-Espanola half, as expected for a branch closed since 1941. Four straight-line bridges cover the rest: ~2.9 miles (4.6km) through the town of Espanola itself, where OSM has no rail tagging under the modern street grid; ~2.8 miles (4.4km) and ~2.7 miles (4.3km) across two gaps through the Rio Grande canyon country south of Espanola (roughly the Otowi/San Ildefonso vicinity); ~4.6 miles (7.4km), the largest single gap, approximating part of the documented 22-mile, 2%-grade descent between Santa Fe and Buckman where no OSM tagging survives at all; and ~0.9 miles (1.4km) for the final approach into the Santa Fe depot area. Every bridge follows the Rio Grande valley / Buckman-grade corridor the line is documented to have used, not a blind straight line between distant towns. No known instance of this feature drawing a later-era alignment than its own years.
